title: Deep learning PET/CT‐based radiomics integrates clinical data: A feasibility study to distinguish between tuberculosis nodules and lung cancer

paragraphs.en: Tuberculosis (TB) is a worldwide infectious disease and the inflammatory cause of death from a single source of infection in the world's top 10 (ranking higher than human immunodeficiency virus/acquired immunodefiniciency syndrome [HIV/AIDS]). 1 In the period between 2019 and 2020, tuberculosis claimed the lives of 1.3 million individuals, nearly double the number of deaths caused by HIV (680000). The medical imaging‐based inflammatory response of tuberculosis (TB) nodules and solid lung cancer (LC) exhibits a high degree of similarity, frequently resulting in misdiagnosis. 2 Misdiagnosis will have an irreversible impact on the diagnosis and treatment of LC. 3 When lung cancer is misdiagnosed as tuberculosis and treated as such, not only will the patient's condition not improve, but it may also lead to lymph node metastasis and distant metastasis. The current 5‐year survival estimates for patients with the seventh edition of non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) range from 73% for stage IA disease to just 13% for stage IV disease. 4 , 5 Improving the accuracy of TB nodules and LC diagnosis is a challenge for clinicians.

18F‐fluorodeoxyglucose (18F‐FDG) and positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) imaging are rapidly becoming crucial diagnostic tools in the investigation of cancer, including its diagnosis, staging, and assessment of recurrence. 6 They can provide tissue function information and morphological density information. 7 , 8 Morikawa et al. reported that lung cancer can present as a parenchymal infiltration resembling pneumonia on chest x‐ray or CT images. 9 It demonstrates that cancer may be misdiagnosed as inflammatory lung disease, thereby delaying accurate diagnosis. Furthermore, the study highlighted that misdiagnosis could result in unnecessary surgeries and a significant financial burden. 10 The probability of false positive results in PET/CT diagnosis of lung cancer was 6.5% and the false positive results of pulmonary tuberculoma was 36.74% in a study by Feng et al. 11 Other studies have also demonstrated that PET/CT is difficult to distinguish between TB nodules and lung cancer. 12 , 13

The development of radiomics has generated significant interest among researchers in recent years and has been applied in various clinical oncology disciplines. 14 , 15 , 16 Radiomics utilizes high‐throughput methods to extract high‐level information from regions of interest (ROI) in images, which are manually segmented by radiologists. 17 Radiology has been demonstrated to be of great value in the diagnosis of human diseases, particularly cancer, in clinical practice. 18 , 19 However, the majority of current radiomic studies are based solely on image heterogeneity information and do not incorporate clinical information. Researchers, such as Gevaert et al., have attempted to create radiomic maps that incorporate molecular pathways by using multilayer linear regression to associate powerful image features. 20 Du et al. have attempted to integrate radiomics and manual features for classification using multiple regression. 21 Muzammil et al. proposed a convolutional sparse image decomposition (CSID) algorithm that merges CT and MR images to extract detailed information. 22 However, the integration model relies on traditional machine learning models that are limited in their ability to process high‐dimensional data and learn complex functions in high‐dimensional space. 23

At the same time, new deep learning technologies have higher levels of abstraction and data integration capabilities. For example, Vijayarani et al. used a deep convolutional neural network (DCNN) to classify liver diseases, such as cirrhosis, bile ducts, chronic hepatitis, liver cancer, and acute hepatitis, based on a liver function test data set. 24 Khan et al. improved the accuracy of lung nodule detection by concatenating deep learning features with handcrafted features, such as gray level co‐occurrence matrix (GLCM) and local binary pattern (LBP). 25 Patch‐based deep learning for lesion classification can also achieve accurate classification with small datasets. 26 , 27 , 28 The integration of deep learning models with radiomics is becoming increasingly common in the processing of medical image information. However, multi‐input deep learning models that integrate multidimensional information are infrequently reported in the literature.

The objective of this study was to evaluate the classification performance of radiomic features, whilst also incorporating image and clinical information as reference factors for the classification of TB nodules and LC. It is important to note that the primary focus of this study was not to differentiate between general tuberculosis and lung cancer, but to examine specific cases. The tuberculosis nodules included in this study were extreme cases, necessitating the use of 18F‐FDG PET/CT and pathological confirmation to eliminate the possibility of lung cancer. Currently, cancer classification surveys tend to focus on separate fields such as imaging, clinical biochemistry, and genetic analysis. The integration of multidomain information in tumor analysis and studies holds promising prospects. The significance of this study was to improve the accuracy of the distinction between TB nodules and LC by combining information from radiomic features, deep learning features, and clinical information. The workflow of this study is illustrated in Figure 1.

This was a retrospective analysis and all patient information has been deidentified, thus ethical review was not necessary. The study was conducted using medical records of patients diagnosed between January 2013 and March 2019 at the hospital. The study sample included 77 cases of pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) nodules and 97 cases of lung cancer (LC). For inclusion in the study, patients had to meet the following criteria: (i) Availability of complete 18F‐FDG PET/CT images; (ii) active pulmonary TB nodules or primary LC confirmed through biopsy or surgical pathology; (iii) presence of solid lesions; (iv) lesions with a maximum diameter of less than 3 cm. Exclusion criteria included: (i) Prior treatment history; (ii) extensive calcification. It is worth noting that extensive calcification is also an important indicator for distinguishing benign from malignant tumors in clinical practice; (iii) history of TB nodules or tumors; (iv) concurrent presence of both pulmonary TB nodules and LC. The data collection process is shown in Figure 2.

The acquisition of PET/CT images was performed in accordance with the guidelines of the European Association for Nuclear Medicine. The images were collected using a Biograph 18F‐FDG PET/CT scanner. The CT scan was acquired prior to the PET scan, with parameters of 120 kVp, automatic tube current modulation of 64–321 mA, and pitch of 0.8 mm. The CT image reconstruction parameters were in‐plane resolution of 0.82 × 0.82 mm2, slice thickness of 1.5 mm, slice spacing of 1 mm, and convolution kernel B70f. The 3D mode PET scan was acquired for 2 min per bed position and was reconstructed using the ordered‐subset expectation maximization (OSEM) algorithm with point spread function (PSF) modeling (3 iterations, 21 subsets). Attenuation and scatter correction were performed using CT transmission data. Post‐reconstruction smoothing was applied using a 4‐mm full width at half maximum (FWHM) Gaussian filter. The post‐reconstruction parameters of the PET images were in‐plane resolution of 4.07 × 4.07 mm2, slice thickness of 5 mm, and slice spacing of 3 mm. The images were then converted to normalized uptake values (SUV) based on bodyweight for analysis.

The CT and PET image data were processed using the SimpleITK library in Python. The images were first resampled to an isotropic standard image with a voxel spacing of 1:1:1. To normalize the gray values of the images, the mean and standard deviation specification method was used. Finally, the processed images were saved in the Neuroimaging Informatics Technology Initiative (NII) format.

Table 1 summarizes the collected clinical information for each patient. Clinical information features were extracted by two nuclear medicine physicians with over 10 years of experience in PET/CT diagnosis. The results were obtained independently, and in case of any discrepancies, they were resolved through group discussion. The clinical data, obtained from experienced clinicians, includes patient demographic information such as gender and age, as well as lesion‐specific information such as lesion location, diameter, presence of cavities, vacuoles, burrs, and vascular clusters. A vacuole is a hollow vesicle‐like structure filled with fluid. Burrs refers to a small spine‐like structure seen on imaging. Vascular cluster refers to a structure formed by multiple blood vessels together. Additionally, the lobes and calcification status, as well as the metabolic activity and longitudinal diaphragmatic blood pool of the lesions were recorded. Longitudinal diaphragmatic blood pool is a nuclear medicine imaging technique used to evaluate the blood flow in the heart and major blood vessels by injecting a radiotracer, typically 99mTc red blood cells. The radioactivity status was also recorded, with highly active lesions being marked as 1 and inactive lesions being marked as 0.

The PET/CT images were processed using open‐source annotation software ITK‐SNAP (version 3.6.0; www.itksnap.org) for manual segmentation. The tumor boundary was marked layer by layer by a radiologist with 3 years of experience and re‐examined by a radiologist with 10 years of experience for accuracy. The lesions are marked in the region of interest (ROI), as shown in Figure 3, and in red. Radiomic features of PET and CT were extracted from the ROI and their 3D reconstruction images were reconstructed.

The extraction of radiomic features was performed using the open source and free pyradiomics package (https://pyradiomics.readthedocs.io/), which is part of the Python library. 29 This package is compliant with the reference standards for radiological analysis and is easily reproducible. As demonstrated in Figure 1, 100 radiomic features were extracted from the respective PET/CT lesion areas, in accordance with the guidelines set by the International Biomarker Standards initiative (IBSI). 30 , 31 The radiomic features were extracted from 97 LC patients and 77 TB nodule patients, with each patient's nodule selected as the region of interest (ROI) in the image. We selected the specific radiomic features based on standardized guidelines and recommendations provided by the IBSI and pyradiomics. A total of 19 first‐order statistics, 16 features based on 3D shape, 24 gray level co‐occurrence matrix (GLCM) features, six gray level run length matrix (GLRLM) features, 16 gray level zone area matrix (GLSXM) features, five neighborhood gray tone difference matrix (NGTDM) features, and 14 neighborhood gray level dependent matrix (NGLDM) features were extracted from the respective PET and CT images. The manual segmentation was performed separately on the CT and PET images. Radiomic features were extracted from both CT and PET images, and then combined using a radiomic pipeline to create a comprehensive feature set. As shown in Figure 4a, in order to avoid overfitting, we used the lasso regression method to select 12 radiomic features, and then further removed two highly correlated radiomic features, gray level size zone matrix (Glszm) zone entropy and gray level co‐occurrence matrix (Glcm) joint entropy with a correlation coefficient greater than 0.8 using Pearson's correlation coefficient. Finally, we obtained 10 radiomic features as shown in Figure 4b.

The patches of the input image were resized to a fixed size of 50 × 50 voxels using bilinear interpolation. The structure of the convolutional neural network was based on the classic ResNet structure, which has been shown to provide more accurate object recognition. 32 Mascarenhas and Agarwal compared the commonly used convolutional neural network structures of VGG16, VGG19, and ResNet50 and found that the ResNet structure was best suited for image classification. 33

As shown in Figure 5, the deep learning feature extraction module is based on the ResNet architecture. A fully connected layer is utilized as a feature extractor, followed by an average pooling layer which serves as the connection to the classifier module. Subsequently, a dense layer of elements are connected and the sigmoid function is utilized to normalize the output value between 0 (representing 100% TB) and 1 (representing 100% LC). The input to the model consists of segmented PET and CT image patches. The model trains using the training set and is evaluated using the test set. If the assessment of the model improves from the previous iteration, the updated model is saved.

The integrated model was implemented using the Keras library (https://keras.io/). As shown in Figure 5, the integrated model integrates radiomic features, clinical information, and deep learning features to construct a unified system. The model consists of three separate modules, each of which processes image data, radiology data, and clinical data, respectively. A total of 1024 features are extracted by these modules. Additionally, the model has a feature selection function, which will be discussed in the discussion section. To summarize, the three sets of features are not simply summed but are processed through feature selection and extraction. It is noteworthy that after the integration of these three sets of features, no additional complex structures are employed. The goal is to make full use of the feedforward algorithm of the neural network, and to facilitate efficient feedback information flow to the feature extraction modules.

The region of interest, defined as the region of the lesion, was analyzed to extract 100 radiomic features from both the CT and PET images using the pyradiomics package. These features were then concatenated and transformed into a vector format. 90% of the features were used for training, while the remaining 10% were utilized for testing. A random forest algorithm, known as traditional radiomics, was selected for the analysis. As shown in the blue part of Figure 5, both the PET and CT images were input into a residual neural network, with the resulting deep learning features directly fed into the classification module. Additionally, the radiomic features were combined with the deep learning features in the classification module, which was used to predict the classification of TB nodules and LC.

The present study investigated the performance of traditional radiomics, DCNN, radiomics‐DCNN, and integrated model models. The statistical software used was python (3.6) and Statistical Program for Social Science (SPSS 36.0). p‐values less than 0.05 were statistically significant. The training and test sets were randomly divided into 9:1. The χ2 test of clinical data verified group differences (categorical variables). For age and tumor diameter, t‐test was used to verify group differences (continuous variables). The results are shown in Table 1. In order to assess the consistency and robustness of the results generated by our model, 10‐fold cross‐validation was implemented. A range of evaluation metrics were used to evaluate the performance of the models, including accuracy (ACC), specificity (SPE), sensitivity (SEN), F1‐score, and the area under curve (AUC) as well as the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve.

The study employed the bilinear interpolation method to resize the PET/CT image data to 50 × 50 voxels. The final image size of 50 × 50 × 100 was obtained by concatenating the PET and CT images along the channel dimension. The model's optimizer was set to Adam with a learning rate of 0.0001 and a decay of 0.01 for each training cycle. The loss function used was “binary cross entropy” and the evaluation metric used for each training epoch was the accuracy (ACC). The training process was run for a total of 100 epochs.

As shown in Table 2, the classification performance of traditional radiomic classification (traditional radiomics) and DCNN relying on deep learning feature signals and convolutional neural network (radiomics‐DCNN) relying on radiomic signals and deep learning features signals and deep learning of the integrated radiomic signals convolutional neural network (integrated model) relying on radiomic signals, deep learning features signals and clinical information were evaluated. The AUC value of the integrated model was 0.84 (0.82–0.88), which was better than other models.

Both traditional radiomics with an AUC of 0.76 (0.75–0.78) and DCNN with an AUC of 0.72 (0.67–0.81) performed worse than intuitive diagnosis. It indicates that the classification ability of relying solely on radiomic signals or deep learning feature signals was lower than radiologists. The AUC value of radiomics‐DCNN was 0.82 (0.81–0.84) significantly higher than the previous two models, indicating that the integration of radiomic feature signals and deep learning feature signals can improve the classification ability of TB nodules and LC. The performance of radiomics‐DCNN and the integrated model classification were better than traditional radiomics and DCNN models in ACC, SEN, SPE, F1‐score, AUC evaluation indicators. More importantly, the integrated model was superior to the intuitive diagnosis, which will have clinical significance for the diagnosis of TB nodules and LC. The AUC value of the integrated model was 0.84 (0.82–0.88), which is better than the other three models. The results of the t‐test show that the integrated model was significantly higher than other models.

The results of the different models are shown in the ROC curves presented in Figure 6. It is evident that the integrated model exhibits superior classification ability in comparison to other models. This demonstrates the efficacy of combining clinical information and image information in the diagnosis and differentiation of TB nodules and LC. The results show that the AUC of the best performing integrated model (0.88) was significantly higher than that of models which only depend on individual inputs. We conducted the DeLong test, and the results show that there was a significant difference (p < 0.05) between the integrated model and the other three models.

The objective of this study was to enhance the accuracy of differentiation between TB nodules and LC through the application of deep learning techniques, thereby providing valuable insights for medical practitioners during the diagnostic process. The key contribution of this study is the design of a new deep learning model as the classifier, which is believed to be better equipped to integrate information from different dimensions. The proposed deep learning model integrated multiple dimensions of information, including radiomic features, deep learning features, and clinical data.

A phenomenon has been noticed that models based solely on radiomic signals basically have high false positives. The same problem has also been frequently reported in computer‐aided inspection systems based on traditional machine learning models. 34 , 35 This problem may be caused by the fact that the model only relies on a single signal. Deep learning models have powerful feature generalization and learning capabilities. They can comprehensively utilize different dimensions of information such as images and radiomic features. At the same time, deep learning models have also been reported to reduce the false positives of solid tuberculosis detection. 36 Ioannis et al. combined deep learning and machine learning models for the diagnosis of cardiovascular disease. 37 The results show that the combined InceptionV3 and random forest models match the accuracy to 79.15% on the specific dataset. It has been demonstrated that the combined model of multiple inputs outperforms the model of individual signals, which is consistent with our results. Li et al. combined radiomic and clinical informative features to distinguish three histological subtypes of lung cancer. 38 However, the study yielded the opposite result. The possible reason is that the classifiers in this study are all traditional machine learning models, which cannot fully integrate information from different dimensions. 39

The deep learning model was selected for the following reasons: (i) Deep convolutional neural network features are better than traditional manual features, (ii) deep learning networks can combine feature extraction modules and classification modules for end‐to‐end training and (iii) multidimensional information can be processed as a deep learning model. 40 The feature extractor of the revised ResNet structure was specifically designed to extract deep learning features from PET/CT images and has been reported to be effective in doing so. 24 , 41 The feature extractor consists of two one‐dimensional convolutional layers (15 × 3) followed by a ReLU activation layer and a dense layer with 1024 units. Radiomic and clinical feature signals are fed into this feature extractor with the purpose of extracting relevant features for disease diagnosis and reducing redundant information. 21 , 42 , 43

It is noteworthy that a convolutional neural network structure with multiple inputs for different feature signals was designed. The deep learning features, radiomic features, and clinical information features were all adjusted to the same dimension of 1024 to balance the proportion of each feature signal in the final result. After the integration of these three sets of feature signals, they were directly connected to the classifier. It is convenient to pass the error back to the feature extractor. 44 Subsequently, the parameters of the three feature extractors were adjusted to ensure coordination between the three sets of feature signals.

The Lung Image Database Consortium and Image Database Resource Initiative (LIDC‐IDRI) dataset is funded by the National Cancer Institute. It contains 1018 CT scan images that cover the chest CT scan results of 1010 patients. Each scan was annotated by four radiologists to determine whether it showed signs of malignancy. In addition, the LIDC‐IDRI dataset provides a wealth of metadata, including information such as the patient's age, gender, and medical history. We conducted an evaluation of the classification performance of traditional radiomics, DCNN, and integrated models for benign and malignant pulmonary nodules in the LIDC‐IDRI dataset. The results of this evaluation are presented in Table 3. A total of 730 pulmonary nodules were included in the testing dataset. Additionally, the dataset contained clinical information such as margin, calcification, sphericity lobulation, subtlety, spiculation, and texture features for the nodules, which were used as part of the classification process.

It can be concluded that the deep learning model with coordinated input of radiomic signals and deep learning feature signals performs better than the deep learning model with separate input of deep learning signals. Mu et al. proposed a PET/CT‐based deep learning model to predict non‐small cell epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations. 45 The AUC of the model with the combined input of clinical features and deep learning features was 0.8, which has better performance than the model with the input of deep learning features alone, and is similar to our conclusion. The multi‐input coordinated deep learning model has also been reported to have achieved good results in the classification of different tumors. 46 , 47 This model achieves high AUC in the model based on the image features of PET and CT compared to other studies. 48 , 49

In this study, all variables related to the classification were evaluated, including clinical feature signals, deep learning feature signals, and radiomic signals. However, only the impact of adding dimension signals on the performance of deep learning models was considered, and the impact of different combinations of signals was not addressed. The ResNet structure model was used to extract deep learning features based on its successful application in image feature extraction. However, finding a better model structure for deep learning feature extraction remains a challenge for future studies. Moreover, the data set used in this study was relatively small, which could limit the performance of the model. To address this issue, future studies should aim to collect a larger TB and clinical dataset or modify the model structure to better accommodate small data sets. 50 , 51

In conclusion, in this study, an integrated model was developed for the purpose of differentiating between pulmonary tuberculosis and lung cancer. It combined deep learning feature signals, radiomic signals, and clinical feature signals for improved performance. The use of multiple input deep learning models has been shown to be more effective for the classification of lung cancer and pulmonary nodules compared to models with single inputs. The integrated model is capable of providing valuable auxiliary diagnostic information to assist physicians in accurately distinguishing between TB nodules and LC. The experiment results demonstrate the effectiveness of integrating information from multiple modalities for improved disease diagnosis accuracy.
